title: Hebrew Feature Across Two Models
takeaway: The Hebrew feature from run A has a counterpart in a second, independently trained run that fires on nearly the same tokens (activation correlation 0.92) but whose effects on next-token logits agree far less (0.3). The paper reads that gap the way it read the same gap for the Arabic feature: the tokens the feature is actually about agree closely, while a large central cloud of near-zero logit weights, which the paper guesses is unwanted interference, drags the overall correlation down.
walkthrough:
Two scatter plots compare one feature against its match in a second model. The left panel compares when the two fire; the right panel compares what they do to predictions.

Both plots name the same pair, `A/1/416` vs `B/1/1901`. In the paper's notation the letter is the transformer, the middle digit is the [[dictionary-learning-run]], and the last number picks a feature out of that run. `A/1/416` is the [[hebrew-feature]]. `B/1/1901` comes from a run over a different transformer, trained on the same data with a different random seed — which is what makes this a test of [[universality]].

### How to read the left panel

Each dot is one token from the sampled data. Its horizontal position is the [[feature-activation]] of `B/1/1901` there; its vertical position is the activation of `A/1/416`. Color is the [[hebrew-script-proxy]], a [[computational-proxy]] scoring how Hebrew-looking the token is: red is high, blue is low.

The stacked strips along each axis are marginals — the activation histogram of one run alone, broken down by that same proxy. The narrow strip at `0`, cut off by a `>0` break, holds the tokens where the feature does not fire at all, which is nearly all of them.

Points climb along a diagonal, and the dense red blob near the top right is the Hebrew mode: both runs fire hard on the same Hebrew tokens. Their [[pearson-correlation]] here, the paper's [[activation-similarity]], is 0.92.

### How to read the right panel

Now each dot is a vocabulary token, and its coordinates are the [[logit-weight]] each run's feature places on it — how much that feature's firing pushes that token's logit.

There are two modes. A small pink-circled cluster labeled "Hebrew Token Logits" sits at the top right: both runs strongly upweight the same Hebrew tokens. A much larger blue cloud sits around the origin, labeled "Interference Weights?".

That cloud is why [[logit-weight-similarity]] is only 0.3. The paper's guess — and the question mark is theirs — is [[weight-interference]]: under [[superposition]] feature directions cannot all be orthogonal, so [[interference]] forces small nonzero weights the model would rather have at zero.

The same split, with the same explanation, appeared for the [[arabic-script-feature]].

terms.definition: The left plot compares the two features by when they fire — their scalar ReLU activations, token by token, over a sample of the dataset.
The right plot compares the two features by what they do — the vector, one entry per vocabulary token, of how much the feature's firing raises or lowers that token's next-token logit.
The Hebrew feature under study: feature index 416 in dictionary learning run 1 over transformer A. It fires with high specificity on Hebrew script in the upper part of its activation range.
Feature index 1901 in run 1 over transformer B, found as the feature in B whose activations correlate most highly with A/1/416's. It is the candidate counterpart the figure is testing.
Two one-layer transformers trained on the same dataset with different random seeds, each given its own dictionary learning run with otherwise identical hyperparameters.
Which of the two runs an axis belongs to. The y-axis of both panels is always run A's feature; the x-axis is always run B's.

terms.term: Correlation between A and B (subtitle line)
terms.definition: The Pearson correlation of the points plotted in that panel — of the two activation vectors on the left, of the two logit weight vectors on the right.
How strongly B/1/1901 fires on each sampled token.
How strongly A/1/416 fires on the same token. Printed on the figure as 'Feature Activaitons', a typo in the original.
The weight B/1/1901 places on a given vocabulary token's logit.
The weight A/1/416 places on that same vocabulary token's logit.

terms.term: Red points and red histogram regions
terms.definition: Tokens the Hebrew script proxy scores high, i.e. tokens it judges to be Hebrew text. On the right panel, red marks Hebrew vocabulary tokens.

terms.term: Blue points and blue histogram regions
terms.definition: Tokens the proxy scores low — everything it does not judge to be Hebrew. The intermediate blue shades are middling proxy scores, since the proxy is a continuous log-likelihood-ratio score rather than a yes/no label.

The stacked-area bands running along the left and bottom edge of each panel: the one-dimensional distribution of that axis's quantity on its own, colored by proxy score. They show specificity for one run without reference to the other.

A break separating the exactly-zero activations, held in a thin strip, from the positive ones. It is there because the vast majority of the probability mass sits at zero — features are sparse — and would otherwise flatten the rest of the plot.

terms.term: Hebrew Token Logits (right-panel annotation, pink ellipse)
terms.definition: The hand-drawn ring around the small upper-right cluster of vocabulary tokens that both features strongly upweight. These are Hebrew characters and the partial UTF-8 byte tokens that make them up.
The ring around the large near-zero cloud, with the authors' own question mark. Their hypothesis is that these weights are noise the model is forced into by superposition, not deliberate behavior.
Reference lines at logit weight 0 on each axis, splitting the plot into quadrants so that agreement in sign can be read off directly.

The paper's model-independent way of comparing features by treating each as a vector of values over a fixed set of datapoints and correlating those vectors. It is the number reported over the left panel.
The second comparison: treat each feature as a vector indexed by vocabulary token, holding its logit weights, and correlate. It is the number reported over the right panel.

The byte token that begins the UTF-8 encoding of most characters in the basic Hebrew Unicode block. It is one of the tokens in the upper-right logit cluster, and a separate feature, A/1/1016, specializes in predicting the byte that completes it.

numbers.meaning: Activation correlation between A/1/416 and B/1/1901 — the number printed above the left panel. It is high because both runs fire hard on the same Hebrew tokens and stay near zero elsewhere, which is the paper's evidence that the Hebrew feature is universal across the two models.

Logit weight correlation between the same two features, printed above the right panel. It is much lower than 0.92 not because the Hebrew tokens disagree — those sit together in the top-right cluster — but because the plot is numerically dominated by thousands of near-zero weights that agree only loosely.

The corresponding pair for the Arabic feature (A/1/3450 vs B/1/1334), shown earlier in the paper. The Hebrew pair reproduces the same shape: activation correlation near 0.9, logit weight correlation far below it. The caption's word 'again' refers to this.

The range of both activation axes. Both features top out near 8, and the shared Hebrew mode sits roughly between 4.5 and 6.5 on run B and 6 and 8 on run A — run A's feature reaches somewhat higher values for the same tokens, which is why the main blob sits above the diagonal.
The range of both logit weight axes. The scale is small because a logit weight is a per-token push, and most tokens get almost none.
Where the circled Hebrew token cluster sits. Both features push these tokens up by a similar, comparatively large amount, which is the agreement the paper cares about.

The extent of the central 'Interference Weights?' cloud. It holds the bulk of the vocabulary. The ellipse drawn around it is tilted, so these weights are not entirely uncorrelated here — but the tilt is weak enough that the cloud pulls the overall correlation down toward 0.3.
The number of tokens over which activation correlations are computed when searching run B for the feature best matching one in run A. B/1/1901 was picked as the argmax of that correlation.

Context from the paper's global analysis: the median activation correlation between a feature in A/1 and its best match in B/1 is 0.72, while the same procedure on transformer neurons gives 0.46. The Hebrew pair's 0.92 sits well above the typical feature.

The Pearson correlation between A/1/416 and the Hebrew script proxy — the coloring rule used in this figure. It is well short of 1, partly because a complementary feature, A/1/1016, handles the \xd7 byte, so the red/blue split should be read as an imperfect label rather than ground truth.

numbers.value: 1 (the middle digit in A/1 and B/1)
numbers.meaning: Both features come from dictionary learning run number 1 of their respective models. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient, so matching the run number keeps the comparison between like and like.
